Australia clinched a convincing 214-run win over South Africa in the first Test of their three-match series to take a 1-0 lead.

Australia went into the final day in Durban requiring six more wickets to clinch victory, and South Africa a hugely unlikely 319 more runs to win, and though the visitors encountered some resistance from Aiden Markram (75) in particular, they eventually wrapped things up shortly after lunch.

Josh Hazlewood (6-49) took three of the wickets to fall to finish with career-best figures, including the opening breakthrough of Wiaan Mulder (29) to end his and Markram's 69-run stand that offered South Africa some brief hope of clinging on for a draw.

articles.headline: Ranking the NBA's top 100 players: Victor Wembanyama enters 2026-27 season at No. 1
keyFacts: Victor Wembanyama is ranked as the number one NBA player entering the 2026-27 season by CBS Sports analysts.
Six CBS Sports analysts determined the rankings based on expected performance for the upcoming season, including injury considerations.
The 2026-27 NBA season is scheduled to begin in one week.
body: There was a time not so long ago in NBA history when teams believed that they could simply assemble two or three of the top 20 players in the NBA and waltz their way to an NBA championship. Not anymore.
Just consider how the last handful of NBA champions have fared in our annual ranking of the top 100 players in the league:
All five starters from the 2025-26 New York Knicks, plus backup center Mitchell Robinson, were ranked as top 100 players a year ago.
Six members of the 2024-25 Oklahoma City Thunder were selected two seasons ago.
All five starters on the 2023-24 Boston Celtics ranked within the top 62 of that year's list.
The 2022-23 Denver Nuggets placed four players within the top 75.

Your inclination will almost certainly be to focus on the beginning of the list. Who's No. 1? Who's rising into superstardom? What older players are starting to slip? But winning a championship in the 2020s means having players scattered throughout the entire list. You need your superstars, of course, but you need your Josh Harts and your Alex Carusos and your Al Horfords just as badly.

Six CBS sports analysts submitted ballots for this year's list: Brad Botkin, John Gonzalez, Robby Kaland, Jack Maloney, Sam Quinn and Cameron Salerno. The players were ranked on how we expect them to fare in the 2026-27 season, meaning injuries factored in both for players returning from lengthy absences (like Kyrie Irving and Tyrese Haliburton) and ones who will miss time to open the season (like Jimmy Butler).
So, with all of that in mind, let's dive into our ranking of the 100 best players in the NBA entering the 2026-27 season, which tips off in one week.

articles.headline: With UH football on the upswing, there's no reason not to turn out for showdown vs. Oklahoma State
keyFacts: The University of Houston football team hosts No. 18 Oklahoma State this Saturday in a significant Big 12 conference matchup.
Head coach Willie Fritz is encouraging fans to attend the 6:30 p.m. game to help achieve a stadium sellout.
School officials expect attendance to approach 35,000 and have planned special features including a drone show to attract spectators.
body: UH football's last home sellout came against Texas in 2023. Saturday's matchup against Oklahoma State brings the high-stakes game that has been few and far between at TDECU Stadium over the past decade. (Jason Fochtman/Staff photographer)
Willie Fritz will sometimes run the steps, stopping to take in the view of the downtown skyline from the upper deck at TDECU Stadium.
"Every seat is a good seat," the University of Houston 's third-year football coach said. "That's unique this day and age with stadiums."

If Fritz has his way, every seat will be filled (preferably in red) when the No. 20 Cougars host No. 18 Oklahoma State on Saturday in what could be their biggest regular-season home game in more than a decade.
It's a key midseason meeting between two contenders in the Big 12 race.
UH NOTEBOOK: Patrick Overymyer, Liam Dougherty earn accolades
Two explosive offenses.
Two of the nation's top quarterbacks, UH's Conner Weigman and OSU's Drew Mestemaker.
And, for once, it's a 6:30 p.m. game.
"We oughta have a sellout," Fritz said. "That's the goal."
Still not sold?
Just ask Willie the Weatherman.
"It won't be hot," Fritz continued. "It will be nice and cool. I hear it's going to be about 75 degrees."
Sign up for Cougar Confidential
You'll get get in-depth news and analysis about UH's basketball and football teams from reporter Joseph Duarte by signing up for the Cougar Confidential newsletter .

Fritz ticked through his selling points just minutes after Saturday's 35-16 win over Kansas State in Manhattan, Kan. All that was missing was a PowerPoint presentation and a road map for UH fans who might have forgotten the directions after a decade of mostly uninspired football and unattractive matchups.
That was then.
This is now.
That was Conference USA and the American Athletic Conference.
This is the Big 12.
That was Tulsa, East Carolina, UAB, Temple and USF.
This is Power Four football.
Coming off a 10-win season , the Cougars are halfway to that total just two weeks into October. They are among a half-dozen teams bunched together in a tight Big 12 race.
"It's a big game," Fritz said. "It's a big game for them, it's a real big game for us. It has a lot of implications for the Big 12 race. This is a huge game. We're very excited about the challenge."

The stakes haven't been this high for a UH regular-season home game since backup quarterback Kyle Postma helped rally the Cougars from a 20-point deficit to beat Memphis 35-34 late in their 2015 Peach Bowl season.

You have to go back to 1990 for the last time UH hosted a game between two ranked major-conference teams. That year, David Klingler and Chuck Weatherspoon led the No. 12 Cougars to a 36-31 win over No. 20 Texas A&M at the Astrodome.
Fritz would like to make big games the norm.

"That's the reason we came here," Fritz said. "We feel like we can compete for a national championship here at the University of Houston. We've got the facilities. We've got the location. Without question. We're finding out a lot of kids go away and they want to come back. We want to be in this situation all the time."
There have been roadblocks at seemingly every turn, many of them self-inflicted. There's the bitterness , still lingering, of being left out of the Big 12 after the SWC breakup.
Ten losing seasons since the turn of the century, the lowlight the only winless campaign (0-11 in 2001) in program history.

There have been early kickoff times, including the hit-the-snooze-button 11 a.m. window that has often felt like a weekly occurrence. Two of UH's three home games this season, both played in the September heat, kicked off at 11 a.m. UH averaged 27,167 fans for those games, with empty sections at TDECU Stadium beamed to a national audience.
Since the 40,000-seat TDECU Stadium opened in 2014, UH has played before seven sellouts.
Seven .
In 75 games.
"I've played in front of 50 and 110,000," Fritz said.

UH will gladly take somewhere in the middle. Athletic director Eddie Nuñez said the school has planned several in-game features, including a drone show. The pregame SLAB entrance has been a big hit. A school official said attendance could approach 35,000.
A social media post Monday afternoon challenged the student section to reach 10,000.

- Houston Athletics (@UHCougars) October 12, 2026 Fritz said fans should give the Cougars a chance.

"We just feel like if we can get people out here one time, they see what we have to offer and the quality of product that the Big 12 puts out on the field," Fritz said. "I ask people, just come out and give it a chance, and you'll be hooked.
"There's no reason not to come out. I'm looking forward to seeing a bunch of red in the stands."

articles.headline: The Adoring Fan Is Calling You As Oblivion Remastered Hits Lowest Price On PC
keyFacts: The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered is currently available for its lowest price yet on PC.
The remaster features enhanced graphics and includes the Shivering Isles and Knights of the Nine expansions.
Players can purchase a Steam key for the game at a 37% discount through the retailer Fanatical.
body: At the risk of feeling like an elderly Rose at the end of Titanic, it's been a long time since Skyrim came out. The wait for The Elder Scrolls VI has been even longer. I was just 11 years old when I saw a copy of the game on PS3 and was enamored enough with the cover art to give it a try. Now, 15 years later, I'm 26 and still waiting. However, as someone who never got to play the original, The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered is at least giving me my Bethesda fix for the time being. And you can join me in Cyrodiil, as the game has hit its lowest price yet on PC.

Imprisoned in a cell and seemingly destined to rot, your luck changes when Emperor Uriel Septim VII arrives with his guards and uses the secret exit hidden in your jail. As luck would have it, you've been pardoned—lucky you. Not so lucky is the fact that the Emperor's sons have been killed, and the assassins are after him, too. Now you're tagging along with death chomping at your heels. Fortunately, you're not dying today. I can't say the same for Uriel, who gifts you the Amulet of Kings before shuffling off this mortal coil. With your freedom secured and the Emperor dead, the world seems more open than ever. That is, until the Daedra invade Tamriel.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wFJ3PZuAjK4&pp=ygUbb2JsaXZpb24gcmVtYXN0ZXJlZCB0cmFpbGVy

Of course, the main quest is sitting right there, demanding that you save the world and stop the Daedra from invading through Oblivion Gates. But how can you resist helping a paranoid Wood Elf who wants you to tail people and report on their weird behavior? Or getting involved in a party where you can kill all the guests in a variety of creative ways? You could even hunt them down one by one. It's up to you. The Daedra may be taking over the world, but I'm busy. Can they take a rain check?

The remaster isn't just a quick visual touch-up being sold at full price. The graphics have been enhanced across the board, bringing the game closer to modern standards while remaining faithful to the 2006 classic. It also includes the Shivering Isles and Knights of the Nine expansions, making this the complete Cyrodiil experience. As someone who never got to enjoy Oblivion when it was first released, it was great to finally play it—and enjoy a new Elder Scrolls game (to me). Bethesda, where's the sixth entry?

Right now, you can grab The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered for just $31.49 / £31.49 at Fanatical , getting a Steam key at 37% off. That's lower than the game's previous lowest price on Steam. Considering we've been waiting nearly two decades since Oblivion's original release for a new Elder Scrolls game—and over a decade since Skyrim—what else have you got to play? Don't you dare look at the upcoming games and tell me I'm wrong.

articles.headline: God Of War Laufey Collector’s Edition Doesn’t Include The Game, This Time On Purpose
keyFacts: The God of War Laufey Collector’s Edition includes a statue, a card deck, and an art book but does not contain the game.
The collector's box is expected to cost approximately $130, requiring customers to purchase the game separately for an additional $70.
Unlike previous errors with God of War Ragnarok, Sony has made the exclusion of the game in this new collector's edition entirely deliberate.
body: I refuse to allow this to become normal. No matter how many times it happens, it’s completely deranged, and we should keep calling it out.Â God of War Laufey‘s so-called Collector Box has been revealed (thanks PushSquare), containing a light-up statue, a 51-card deck and an art book, and…no copy of the game. Looking likely to cost around $130 (the U.S. version is yet to be announced, but the UK’s version is Â£130), you’ll still have to spend another $70 on top if you want to play the game the box is allegedly about.

First popping up on the Spanish PlayStation Store, the Caja de Coleccionista de God of War Laufey seemed to have leaked early, before other nations starting revealing the same, with the U.S. still to go. The box contains a resin statue of Faye fighting enemies with her long, pointy sword, complete with purple ribbon, accompanied by lit blue cubes for maximum garishness. There’s also a deck of Oracle cards, 51 in total, each with a unique illustration based on Faye’s journey, and apparently capable of Everywhen magic. And last of all there’s the requisite “mini artbook,” because for over $100 you cannot expect a full-size one. And that’s it. That’s a very expensive statuette, deck of cards, and pamphlet, and only more ridiculous when you consider you haven’t actually bought a copy of the game in the process.
Grand Theft Disco

Of course,Â God of War Laufey‘s deal looks positively sensible when compared to Rockstar’s reveal of a $400Â GTA 6 collector’s edition that also doesn’t come with the game. But the practice remains absolutely ludicrous given it’s the difference of putting a piece of paper with a code printed onto it. Given the items in the box can’t cost much more to produce than about $60 at a push, it’s pretty grim that it’s not in there by default, even putting aside the inherent weirdness of it. And unlikeÂ GTA 6,Â Laufey is getting a physical release.

Making this even more strange is the debacle that occurred during the lastÂ God of War‘s release. 2023’sÂ Ragnarok had two different (far better) special editions, the Collector’s and the JÃ¶tnar Edition, both of which were supposed to come with a download code for the full game andâinexplicablyâa steelbook display case that didn’t contain a disc. This then got worse when people discovered the download code hadn’t been included. This was at least an error that Sony worked to resolve, but three years later the absence is now entirely deliberate.

As for why this ever happens, one possible reason is cost-saving. If you are selling the game on multiple consoles, you need to produce multiple versions of the collector’s edition, and that means different SKUs, different box designs, and so on. Except, Laufey is a PS5 exclusive, so this doesn’t apply at all. It simply seems to be an exercise in finding out what can be gotten away with while still making money. At least the box doesn’t contain a disc case to not put a disc in this time, I guess.

articles.headline: Tekken 8 finally gives a first look at upcoming guest Yujiro Hanma from Baki, and he looks just as grotesque as you'd expect
keyFacts: Bandai Namco revealed the first in-game look at Yujiro Hanma from the Baki manga as a guest character for Tekken 8's Season 3 DLC.
The character trailer debuted at Evo France, showcasing Yujiro's muscular design and intro animation within the game's Unreal Engine 5 environment.
A full gameplay trailer for Yujiro Hanma is scheduled to release in January during the Tekken World Tour finals.
body: The main selling point of Tekken 8's Season 3 DLC pass, alongside veterans Kunimitsu, Bob and Roger Jr, is Yujiro Hanma, the main antagonist of fighting manga Baki and father of its eponymous protagonist. Yujiro was initially revealed in May through a trailer made up entirely of panels from Baki, leaving it in question just how a character that looks like that would be adapted into the Unreal Engine 5 hyper-realism of Tekken 8. The answer, apparently, is that Bandai just said fuck it, and let him look inevitably grotesque.

The first look at Yujiro in-game arrived during Evo France (where Marvel Tōkon also revealed a bunch of new fighters), with a trailer featuring just a quick tease of his intro animation. Inexplicable flexibility, absurdly huge musculature and horrifying grin on show, Yujiro is horrible to look at. Which, I guess, is the intent? This is kinda just how he looks in the manga, too, but seeing him alongside the rest of the Tekken cast is very jarring. Some part of me hopes he's low tier just so I can see less of him on tournament streams, but somehow I doubt that'll happen: his whole thing is being The Strongest Creature on Earth, after all.

He's a strange pick for a fighting game character, honestly. Yujiro in the manga bears the lazy narrative trope of simply being 'the strongest', winning any fight because he's Yujiro Hanma, like a child in a playground quickly coming up with excuses for why he wins, actually. There have been characters in fighting games that are unfathomably strong and therefore shouldn't lose before, such as Slayer in Guilty Gear or Saitama in One Punch Man: A Hero Nobody Knows, but those characters are designed to make their losses make sense; Slayer is just toying with his opponent, lazily blocking with one hand as he feels no threat, and Saitama is a guaranteed win button balanced by the fact he takes a long time to enter the fight. Yujiro, from what I can see, doesn't have one of these loopholes: he just cannot lose. I'm really curious to see how his appearance in Tekken 8 deals with this aspect of his character, and seemingly I'll find out in January when his full gameplay trailer drops alongside the Tekken World Tour finals.

Also, as a fun aside, Yujiro has something in common with Heihachi, other than just generally being an awful dad fighting his son forever: throwing his young child off of a cliff to 'test' his resilience. Tekken continues to be the series of bad dads, just no longer limited only to its own universe.

Right now, the best deal on the market is this Gigabyte Gaming A16 Pro with an RTX 5070 Ti for $1,449 (was $2149.99). This is quite possibly the best RTX 5070 Ti deal I've seen for a few months now and one that I would be surprised if it got any cheaper over Black Friday.

I've seen one or two sub-$1,500 RTX 5070 Ti gaming laptops, but they've usually had 16GB of RAM, an older chipset, or some other kind of glaring compromise for the price. In comparison, this machine has 32GB of RAM, an Ultra 7 chipset, and a 1TB SSD, which isn't bad considering the price.

A year ago, we'd see machines like this getting price cuts every week, but it's obviously quite rare these days with laptops being so ridiculously priced. If you're looking for a high-end laptop without breaking the bank, you can do a lot worse than this Gigabyte A16 Pro at Walmart. Not only are you getting a powerful RTX 5070 Ti graphics card and an Ultra Core 7 chipset, but it also features 32GB of RAM right out of the box. While still a little on the pricey end, a massive $700 discount at Walmart makes this one much more affordable this week.

articles.headline: Scientists find evidence of a second-generation planet born from a dying star
keyFacts: University of Warwick astronomers identified evidence of a second-generation planet orbiting a white dwarf star named HS 0209+0832.
Researchers identified the planet by matching decades-old Hubble telescope data to high levels of niobium, an element formed inside dying stars.
Scientists believe the planet will remain in the star's habitable zone for millions of years if the findings are confirmed.
body: Scientists find evidence of a second-generation planet born from a dying star
If confirmed, it would be the first white dwarf found to host a second-generation planet.

Way back in 1999, NASA's Hubble telescope gathered data from a white dwarf star codenamed HS 0209+0832 with 100 chemical features that couldn't be identified. Now, a team of scientists led by astronomers from the University of Warwick has published a paper in Nature, revealing that those chemical features indicate that the white dwarf hosts a second-generation planet.

A white dwarf is what remains of a star like our sun following its red giant phase, wherein it runs out of hydrogen and expands into a massive fireball that's expected to eat up nearby planets, if there are any. It's the dense core left behind after it's done burning up its nuclear fuel and shedding its outer layers.

The planets in our solar system, including the Earth, are all first-generation planets. That means they formed using materials from the birth of the sun. Second-generation planets form from the materials a dying star casts off. They are very, very rare and are mostly suspected to exist around pulsars, which are the highly magnetic and rapidly spinning remnants of dead neutron stars. White dwarfs are more common than pulsars, and Jamie Williams, the lead author of the study, said finding a second-generation planet around one "was completely unexpected."

Williams found evidence of the planet by looking at Hubble's decades-old observations and comparing them to an updated chemical database. They found that the unidentified chemical features matched an element called niobium, which "can only be synthesized in the exotic conditions that briefly emerge inside dying stars." The niobium levels in the system were 1,000 times higher than our sun's, and that amount points to the formation of a planet from the dying star's materials.

The scientists said that the white dwarf is still extremely hot and is still blasting the planet with enough heat to strip out its outer layers. But they believe the planet will stay and that it will remain in the white dwarf's habitable zone for millions of years. According to the European Research Council, which funded the study, HS 0209+0832 would be the first white dwarf found to host a second-generation planet if the team's findings are confirmed.

City players were pictured celebrating with the travelling away fans following full-time at Anfield - after goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki secured the victory - which sparked criticism across social media.

When asked about the celebrations and the comments that followed ahead of facing Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday, Maresca said: "Criticised for what? We won 0-3 at Anfield. What do you want us to do?

articles.headline: Trump 'looking at' firing ambassador to Greece: 'We're not happy'
keyFacts: President Donald Trump said he is considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle following reports alleging improper conduct.

body: President Donald Trump is "looking at" firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after mounting reports alleging improper conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
"Well, we’re looking at it," Trump told reporters at the White House before leaving for an Ohio campaign rally Monday afternoon. "Yeah, we’re not happy."

Trump’s comments came after a senior U.S. official said Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" by reports about Guilfoyle’s conduct and expected to make a decision on her future this week.
TRUMP AND RUBIO WEIGH FIRING KIMBERLY GUILFOYLE AS MISCONDUCT AND DONOR BAILOUT ALLEGATIONS MOUNT

The Wall Street Journal has reported a series of allegations involving Guilfoyle, including that she asked a Trump donor to pay a $100,000 credit card bill before her confirmation hearing while allegedly promising access to administration officials. The Journal also reported claims that Guilfoyle made a threat involving the Greek government, promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company, allowed a lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings and accepted improper gifts or services.
Rubio, who was in Greece last week, was frustrated by reporters repeatedly asking him to address the allegations publicly.
RUBIO SOUNDS CAMPAIGN-READY AS HE RAILS AGAINST OPEN BORDERS, GLOBALISM IN SPEECH FROM ANCIENT GREEK RUINS

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel," Rubio told reporters Thursday at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart Greece, looked on.
"It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things."
BIDEN-ERA DIRECTIVE FOR DIPLOMATS TO PEDDLE DEI ON FOREIGN GOVERNMENTS SCRAPPED BY STATE DEPARTMENT
A day earlier, Rubio said he would not discuss the allegations while visiting a foreign country, but defended the embassy’s work.
"Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job," Rubio said at a joint news conference with the Greek foreign minister. "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."
TRUMP JR UNDER SCRUTINY FROM OWN PARTY OVER PUTIN-LINKED OLIGARCH'S LAVISH GIFT
Vice President JD Vance also weighed in last week, saying he did not know the full details of the specific case but rejected the idea of selling access to government officials.

"Of course, I don’t like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official," Vance told reporters. "I assume you’re talking about a specific case, and I can’t say with confidence that the case you’re talking about is actually reflective of the way you’re describing it."
HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY

Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing through her lawyers. In a statement released late Sunday, attorneys David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall said the money she sought from the Trump donor was payment for public appearances and speaking engagements that predated her nomination.

"Ambassador Guilfoyle has served, and will continue to serve, with integrity, honor and distinction," the lawyers said. "We are evaluating all available legal remedies to collect this debt and any other potential causes of action."

The attorneys also denied impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the department's travel regulations."
BIDEN-ERA FBI TRACKED TRUMP FAMILY TRAVEL AND WILES’ CALLS WITH LAWYERS IN SECRET PROBE: DOCS

A U.S. official told The Associated Press that the State Department's inspector general is looking into the allegations, though it was not clear whether a formal investigation had been opened. The State Department declined to comment to the AP on a potential inspector general probe.
Top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Senate Foreign Relations Committee and House Oversight Committee have called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Guilfoyle is a former California prosecutor who was once married to Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Donald Trump Jr.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.headline: Dead Space creator says he was 'forced to ship' The Callisto Protocol by Krafton: 'We had f*cking Covid'
keyFacts: Glen Schofield stated that publisher Krafton forced him to ship The Callisto Protocol despite development challenges caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.
Schofield claimed the team released 86 patches to address technical issues like framerate stuttering after the game launched to middling critical reception.
The game's performance led to multiple rounds of studio layoffs, and Schofield eventually retired from the video game industry in 2026.
body: "I was forced to ship the game. I'm mad at myself, there's no doubt. I was so stunned by that decision, because we had fucking Covid. A million people died in America. I lost one of my best friends. Every single month, four to six people in my company were getting sick.

"There were times our small team in Spain was shut down; it goes through a small place like that and you lose your rendering team for a while. The main thing you're concerned about, not that you aren't normally, is the health of your team. Making a game just became secondary because this is about life. This is about humanity," via Gameindustry.biz.

Schofield has had a storied career in the games industry. He was the creator and executive producer of Dead Space, but he also worked as a producer on three Call of Duty games, as well as Blood Omen 2: Legacy of Cain.

The Callisto Protocol, developed under Krafton by Striking Distance studios, failed to meet some sky-high expectations after Krafton sank $100 million into the thing. In terms of critical reception, it was fairly middling, although we did give it a very decent 79 in our The Callisto Protocol review.

One of the major things to sink it, though? Framerate stuttering, which led to some brutal negative reviews at launch. It is, to Schofield's credit, the sort of thing that likely could've been ironed out with a few more months of development work. Or alternatively, not being hit by the horrors of a global pandemic midway through development.

This led to layoffs at the studio in August 2023, followed by a further wave in February 2025. Eventually, Schofield retired from videogames entirely in 2026 after his next project couldn't secure funding, commenting that "maybe I've directed my last game."

Later in the Gamesindustry.biz interview, Schofield remarks: "[Krafton] thought Callisto was a complete failure. What they didn't know while all they were doing was complaining, we were doing patches. I waited until I finished all the DLC and put out 86 patches.

"That was a lot of fucking work. Every day you're going in, you're making changes. Some are little, others are massive. That was all to get it back to where it needed to be." The game did release said patches and updates—both to fix the stuttering, and to add new chapters to its story. But alas, it clearly wasn't enough.

US authorities conducted a predawn raid of Omar’s home in Washington, DC, on Monday as part of an ongoing investigation, the Justice Department said.

A person familiar with the investigation said it is related to alleged immigration fraud, and part of the probe concerns the Somali-born lawmaker’s immigration paperwork filled out by her late father when she was a child.
Omar wrote on social media that the US government is being weaponized to target a political enemy of the president.
“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” she said. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

Alvaro Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a one-time ally of ousted Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro.

There is a manic quality to Donald Trump’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s midterm elections to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.

The US president offered to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider backtracking under pressure from the cow lobby. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas.) Following an attack at the Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday that killed 13 people, President Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the group. He had reportedly rebuffed previous requests for help from the kingdom.
"The Houthis are misbehaving very badly. They're misbehaving very badly. No good," Mr. Trump said on Monday.

"If the U.S. becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond, rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the U.S. and all its interests in the region," Houthi political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told the Agence France-Presse news agency in an interview.
He also warned "all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports (should) stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets".
CBS/AFP
Saudis investigate why deadly strike on Riyadh airport wasn't intercepted

Saudi Arabia has launched an investigation to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, including an attack on Riyadh airport that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300, two regional officials said Monday.

The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, said the initial probe showed that Yemen's Houthis first fired multiple drones to pave the way for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles to reach Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport.

The Houthis possess ballistic missiles and advanced systems fitted with warheads that can change direction during flight and pose a challenge to Patriot interceptors and other defense systems used by the Saudis.

One of the officials said the investigation also aims to find out why air defense systems did not provide earlier warning of the attack in which the Houthi missiles and drones flew over 620 miles to reach Riyadh.
Delta delays planned flights from Atlanta to Riyadh amid attacks on airports
Delta Air Lines said Monday it is delaying plans for nonstop flights from Atlanta to Riyadh amid escalating attacks between Yemen's Houthi militants and Saudi Arabia.

"The safety and security of our customers and employees always come first and continue to guide our operational decisions," the company said in a statement. "We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation."

its plans to operate nonstop flights to Riyadh three times a week on its Airbus A350-900 aircraft in October 2026. It said at the time that the new destination would help strengthen business and travel ties between the United States and Saudi Arabia.
The company said Monday the launch of Atlanta-Riyadh flights will take place in March 2027.
Iran's foreign ministry says U.K.'s accusations are unfounded
Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday denied the U.K.'s allegations that Tehran was involved in last month's security incident at a British base used by American bombers.
In a statement posted to social media, the foreign ministry condemned what it said were "unfounded accusations by the United Kingdom against Iran."

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier Monday the security incident at RAF Fairford — which led to the who were later released on bail — was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran" and "almost certainly" by the regime's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
In its response, Tehran said by using terms like "highly likely" and "almost" certain, the U.K. is "hiding behind vague language without presenting concrete evidence or proof."
NATO countries issue joint statement on Iran and RAF Fairford security incident

Foreign ministers of NATO member countries on Monday issued a joint statement condemning "Iran's use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."
The statement said the countries recognize the U.K.'s assertion that last month's , a U.S.-run air base in Britain, was likely coordinated by Iran.

"Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable," the joint statement said. " Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt, and prosecute these acts."

In a separate statement, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said he welcomes the statement issued by allies and partners, echoing their denouncement of "Iran's involvement in violence and threats on Allied territory."
"NATO will continue to do its part to safeguard the security of our one billion people across the Alliance," Rutte said.
Houthis confirm they targeted Riyadh's airport again with ballistic missile
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claimed an attack targeting Riyadh's international airport on Monday, after a Saudi-led coalition said it had shot down a missile over the capital.

"Our armed forces were able to target (King) Khalid International Airport in the Saudi enemy's capital Riyadh this evening with a ballistic missile and the hit was precise," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said. He said the group also targeted the Khamis Mushait base in the kingdom's south with a drone.

Saree also warned against "the consequences of operating flights toward Saudi airports, as they are not safe, with the exception of the airports and airspace of the sacred areas in Mecca al-Mukarramah and Medina al-Munawwarah."
It's unclear whether there were any injuries.
CBS/AFP
Multiple blasts heard in Riyadh, as residents warned of aerial threat
Several powerful explosions rattled the Saudi capital Riyadh on Monday night, just moments after a text message sent to residents' mobile phones warned of an aerial threat.
"The area is under a hostile aerial threat. Please remain calm, stay indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors," read the message.
Around the same time, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its forces intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-backed group at the capital.
"Interception and destruction of a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," Major General Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the coalition, wrote in a post on X.
U.K. foreign minister announces sanctions against 2 Iranian nationals

U.K. Foreign Minister Ed Miliband announced sanctions against two Iranian nationals on Monday, "for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas," he said in a statement.

"We will not tolerate threats on British soil," said Miliband, who earlier had released a joint statement alongside his counterparts in the U.S., Australia, Canada and 23 other countries, which condemned hostile activities by Iran on foreign soil.

Their statements followed a security incident at the RAF Fairford air base in southern England, which U.K. government leaders and others have attributed to Iran. Iran denied its involvement Monday in comments released by state media.
Americans detained for photographing attacks in Saudi Arabia, U.S. embassy says
The U.S. embassy in Riyadh said on Monday that American citizens had been detained for filming recent events in Saudi Arabia, which has suffered a string of deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.

The embassy said "American citizens have been detained for taking photos of recent events," without specifying how many were arrested or whether they had been released. It noted that Saudi authorities have warned that "filming, publishing, or sharing information related to counter missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."
Several foreign residents in Riyadh have told AFP that acquaintances were detained for filming recent events and sharing the footage on social media.
Iran denies involvement in U.K. air base incident, state media reports
Iran on Monday denied any involvement in a security incident at England's RAF Fairford air base, which the U.S. previously used to deploy long-range bombers during the war.

"The Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base," the Iranian state news agency IRNA reported, adding that he "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."
That statement followed earlier remarks from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who said the incident was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
CBS/AFP
Iran claims to have struck 3 supertankers in the Strait of Hormuz in the last 2 days
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Monday to have struck three supertankers in the Strait of Hormuz over the last two days.
The IRGC Navy said in its most recent attack on a ship, Monday, "a third non-compliant super-tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire."

It said the tanker had switched off the system that broadcasts a vessel's location in an effort to evade Iranian restrictions on navigating the strait without permission and "disregarded warnings from the IRGC Navy."

The statement warned that "any cooperation by commercial vessels and oil tankers with the invading, plundering American terrorist and smuggling army in the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf region will be met with a decisive response from us."

President Trump and his senior aides have insisted for weeks that a southern route through the strait, skirting close to Oman's coast, is safe and available, and the U.S. military has escorted an increasing number of ships along that route in recent weeks.
Iran rejects that route and demands that all vessels use a northern passage close to its own coastline, seeking permission from its military.
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center, which monitors incidents in the region, had not reported any attacks on vessels Monday, but it noted at least two projectiles hitting vessels Sunday.
U.S., U.K., Australia, Canada and others condemn Iranian attacks, including "hybrid activities," after air base incident
The foreign ministers of the U.S., the U.K., Australia, Canada and 23 other countries, many in Europe, have released a joint statement condemning hostile activities by Iran on foreign soil.

The statement came on the heels of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying a recent security incident at England's RAF Fairford air base, which was until recently home to U.S. long-range bombers, was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard.

The countries said Monday that they "condemn in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."

Linking the incident to other recent attacks in Europe "targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists, and U.S. interests," the countries said: "Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable."
"Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt, and prosecute these acts."
U.K. prime minister says RAF Fairford air base plot "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran"

The at a British base used by American bombers to strike Iran during the ongoing war was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran" by the regime's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday.

British police have arrested and then released on bail seven men in connection with the alleged plot. The decision to free the men, whom British police say remain under investigation and monitoring, drew , who said in September the incident "might be" linked to Iran.

"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard," Burnham told lawmakers in the U.K. Parliament on Monday.
"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," he added. "We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams."
Burnham said new sanctions against Iran would be announced.
Saudi Arabia vows response after deadly Houthi attacks on airports

Saudi Arabia's energy minister said Monday that the kingdom had been tested, but would mount an "equally serious" response to a string of deadly attacks on Riyadh's international airport by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Lethal airport strikes have rocked the world's top oil exporter since last week, which is pursuing an expensive economic reform drive aimed at attracting foreign investment.

Yemen's, in which a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Houthis, has reignited months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into crisis.

"Energy security can't be taken for granted," Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told an energy conference in Riyadh. "The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious."
Operations remained suspended at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport on Riyadh's outskirts Monday after the weekend's deadly Houthi strikes.

CCTV video of the deadliest strike, which killed 13 people on Saturday, released by Saudi authorities showed Muslim pilgrims in religious attire waiting in departure lounges before a sudden flash tore through the building and brought down flaming debris.
CBS/AFP
Saudi energy minister says petroleum summit shows kingdom still the "energy security capital," despite Houthi attacks

Saudi Arabia will continue implementing its economic goals and investing in energy infrastructure, industrial capacity and international partnerships despite the challenges presented by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said Monday.

Speaking at the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh, the minister said Saudi Arabia had overcome major challenges throughout its history and would continue to do so, insisting that "fear has no place in the Saudi dictionary."

He said Riyadh's hosting of the international event reflected its position as an "energy security capital," adding that the participation of senior officials and experts from around the world showed international confidence in the kingdom and its ability to ensure the safety of visitors.
He spoke as the Saudi capital's main international airport remained shut down after a week of strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen that killed 20 people.

The minister acknowledged that risks to the global energy system had not disappeared and he said that made international dialogue and cooperation essential to protecting supplies and stabilizing markets.

Bin Salman cited the East-West Crude Oil Pipeline as an example of Saudi long-term strategic planning, saying it provided an alternative route to transport oil amid ongoing impediments in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, and that it had helped the kingdom supply global markets during the exceptional circumstances of the war.

He credited state energy giant Saudi Aramco's expertise with helping restore operations quickly when disruptions do occur — which they have on multiple occasions during the U.S.-Iran war. Iran's proxy groups across the Mideast have targeted the East-West pipeline, along with other infrastructure, repeatedly, taking the pipeline out of service for weeks.
Iran arrests lawyer behind death row marriage of protester, say rights groups

Iranian authorities have arrested a lawyer who helped organize and publicize a prison marriage between a young man who was executed the following day over the 2026 anti-government protests and his fiancee, who was also in jail, rights groups said Monday.

Alireza Sepahi, 25, and his partner Mahshad Kashani, 22, were married in a ceremony conducted over the telephone by their lawyer and attended by their fathers on the eve of Sepahi's execution on Oct. 5.
Both were arrested and were being held in separate prisons in the central city of Isfahan over their participation in the nationwide .

Lawyer Amirsalar Davoudi was arrested Sunday by plainclothes forces while attending a hearing at the Isfahan Revolutionary Court to defend Kashani, who is serving a five-year prison term, the Dadban Iranian legal affairs monitor said, according to French news agency AFP.
"Criminal prosecutions against lawyers - particularly those handling political, security, and human rights cases - have in recent years become an ongoing pattern," it said.
The arrest was also confirmed by the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), which said Davoudi's whereabouts were unclear.

Rights groups say Iran has in recent months executed 34 people in connection with the January protests in a bid to intimidate society and prevent further demonstrations. In 2025, the country doubled its use of executions, according to .
BY: CBS/AFP
Saudi capital's airport to remain closed following deadly weekend strikes by Houthis

Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation on Monday extended the temporary closure of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh after it was struck by Houthi missiles twice over the weekend in attacks that killed 14 people .

GACA said in a statement that it would extend the suspension of all operations at the capital's airport "to complete the necessary procedures to verify the safety of the airport's facilities and their operational readiness, in coordination with the relevant authorities."

The airport has been closed since Saturday, when a Houthi strike killed 13 people, including a U.S. citizen. One more civilian was killed Sunday in a subsequent strike, and attacks last week by the Iran-backed rebel group killed six people.
Iran says U.S. and Israel responsible for Strait of Hormuz disruption
Iranian Foreign Minister Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei blamed the U.S. and Israel on Monday for the ongoing disruption to commercial shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
During his weekly press briefing, Baghaei noted that before the U.S. and Israel launched joint airstrikes on Iran at the end of February, the Strait of Hormuz was open.

"Everything we are witnessing in the region" was a result of the "actions of the United States and the Israeli regime," including the economic consequences of the disruption to shipping through the strait, Baghaei said.

"If the governments that are concerned about this situation are genuinely serious about their concerns, they should address the party responsible for creating this situation and seize every opportunity to compel the United States to stop its acts of aggression," he said.
Tehran and Washington both claim to have control over the strait, and they are imposing competing blockades in the Persian Gulf and the strait.
President Trump has on Iran, but has recently stressed it as a necessary means of ensuring the regime in Tehran cannot build a nuclear weapon.
Houthis step up battle to seize major city of Taiz from Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces

Houthi fighters have ramped up their siege of the Yemeni city of Taiz, where fighting has killed more than 60 people in the past 24 hours, military sources from both sides told the French news agency AFP on Monday.

The Houthis have blocked all exits from the city - a major urban center in Yemen's southwest that, if it falls to the Iranian proxy force, would give the Houthis a strategic foothold from which to threaten the de facto Yemeni government capital of Aden, further to the south.
The fighting over the last day alone has killed at least 22 pro-government forces and 40 Houthi fighters, the sources said. The Houthi sources told AFP reinforcements were being sent to the area.
On Sunday, health officials warned of a "humanitarian catastrophe" in Taiz, with medicine, medical equipment and fuel "on the verge of running out."
Taiz is inland from the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where the Houthis captured swathes of territory in a rapid offensive last month.
CBS/AFP
Brent crude oil price creeps back over $105 a barrel despite Trump's Russian diesel announcement
The price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, was trading over $105 a barrel early Monday, hitting a two-week high despite President to .

Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Friday that he'd struck a deal to buy diesel during a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, aiming to tamp down a spike in fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections.

But the plan runs counter to U.S. efforts to cut the flow of money Russia gets from oil and gas sales that can be used to pay for its . A bipartisan group of six U.S. senators called Sunday for the administration to "immediately reverse course" on the plan.
Early Monday, the price of Brent crude edged up about 1% on the day to just over $105 per barrel, while U.S. benchmark crude climbed by a similar amount to just over $92.
CBS/AP
Iran-backed Houthis blame Saudi Arabia for new strikes
Airstrikes targeted two districts in Yemen's Houthi-held capital of Sanaa, the Iran-backed rebel group said Monday, accusing Saudi Arabia of launching the attacks around midnight local time.
A spokesman for Yemen's Houthi-run health ministry said the strikes killed one person and wounded 12 others in Sanaa.

Ministry spokesman Anees al-Asbahi said a strike on a salt factory in Sanaa's Hamadan district killed one man and wounded eight people. A separate strike on a house wounded a woman and three children, he said.
The rebels' media center said Saudi Arabia carried out the strikes, which came as the Houthis continued to fire missiles and drones at the Saudi capital's primary airport and other infrastructure.

Those attacks have killed at least 20 people at Saudi airports over the last week, including three killed on Oct. 6 and 7 at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport; three killed at King Khalid on Oct. 8; 13 people killed by the deadliest single strike on Riyadh's airport Saturday; and one who died in the latest attack on the facility on Sunday.
Saudi Arabian authorities did not immediately confirm their latest strikes in Yemen, but the kingdom has been battling the Iran-backed Houthi rebels for more than a decade in the country.
CBS/AP
Iran says it's still reviewing U.S. response to 7-day ceasefire proposal and indirect talks continue

Iran's Foreign Minister spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Monday that Tehran was still reviewing the U.S. response to a ceasefire proposal Iran put on the table last month, and that the regime continues communicating via mediators.

"I can tell you that the exchange of messages between Iran and the United States through mediators is continuing," Baghaei said, adding that there had "already been considerable discussion of the seven points" in the proposal.

Late last month Iran presented a ceasefire proposal that calls for Tehran to lift its restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and to resume talks on its nuclear program in seven days if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observes a ceasefire that includes Lebanon.
President Trump has publicly rejected the Iranian offer, but negotiations have continued between the two sides via mediators.
U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia urges "extreme caution" in country's airports

The U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia on Monday urged American citizens to exercise "extreme caution" when using all major airports in the country, following a weekend of strikes that killed a total of 13 people.

"The U.S. Mission is aware of additional attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and targeted attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on October 11," the embassy said in a statement.
"Please take extreme caution when using all major airports in Saudi Arabia," it added.
U.S. fighter jet strikes, disables commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman, Pentagon says
The U.S. military disabled a Panama-flagged commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman Saturday by firing on it with a fighter jet, the U.S. military's Central Command said.
According to CENTCOM, the fighter jet fired a "precision munition" at the Ocean Molica, also known as the "Arika Sun," that disabled the "ship's propulsion without harming the crew."
The ship had recently departed an Iranian port. Iran's ports have been under a U.S. blockade since a ceasefire between the two countries collapsed in July.
Four commercial vessels have been disabled by U.S. forces and 135 ships have been turned around since the blockade took effect on July 14, CENTCOM said.
During that period, U.S. forces have also destroyed 10 tankers that are believed to be part of a "shadow fleet" that transports sanctioned Iranian oil and petroleum products, CENTCOM said.
Saudi airport passenger terminal is struck again, a day after 13 were killed

A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 13 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.
Saudi authorities said one person, described as a Pakistani national, was killed, and 11 were injured in the latest attack on the domestic terminal complex at King Khalid International Airport.

The airport - struck four times in the past five days - has been closed since Saturday's missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically.
One American citizen was among the victims of Saturday's strike, the U.S. embassy in Riyadh said.
CBS/AP
U.S. "may" join Saudi strikes on Houthis, Trump says
President Trump left open the possibility the U.S. will join Saudi Arabia's battle against the Iran-backed Houthis on Saturday.

"We may. We're gonna look at it," Mr. Trump said when asked about the possibility as he left the White House for a campaign rally in Tennessee. "We just found out about the recent attack [on the airport]. So we'll make a decision– we move very quickly."
Mr. Trump was also asked about whether the Houthi strike on Riyadh's airport would change his previously announced decision not to launch any potential strikes on Iran until after the midterms.
"Well, we're gonna take a look," he responded.

Multiple people were injured in a strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Saturday. The Houthis have not claimed responsibility for the attack, but Saudi Arabia's aviation authority said the strike was part of "continued attacks targeting civil aviation facilities in the Kingdom."

articles.headline: Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia visit Ceuta
keyFacts: Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited Ceuta to meet with leaders and residents following a summer border incident.
In late July, more than 140 people were killed when some 70,000 refugees rushed the border fence with Spain.
It remains to be seen how Rabat will react to King Felipe's trip amid diplomatic tensions between Spain and Morocco.
body: King Felipe VI and his wife Queen Letizia arrived in Ceuta on Tuesday afternoon to talk to local leaders and meet with residents still dealing with a major incident at the border with Morocco over the summer.
The trip marks the first royal visit to Ceuta, and Spain's other exclave in the area Melilla, since Felipe's father Juan Carlos I toured the cities in 2007.
Excited crowds gathered to welcome the royals, with some noting that it felt like national authorities were finally paying attention to their plight.
What happened in Ceuta?
In late July, some 70,000 refugees in Morocco rushed the border fence with Spain. More than 140 people were killed in the scuffle.

The incident threw the city of some 84,000 residents into the international spotlight, with calls from right-wing governments within the European Union to suspend the Schengen free movement agreement with Spain.

However, it soon became clear that most of the refugees were quickly turned back to Morocco, and because of Ceuta's remote location, none moved on to mainland Europe except a group of at-risk children.

At the same time, locals complained that national officials did little to help with at least 10,000 migrants still in the city, and the alleged human traffickers trying to capitalize on the situation.
Meanwhile, the migrants who have been unable to return to Morocco have accused Spanish police of brutality and other abuses.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has accused organized groups stemming from Russia and Israel for spreading misinformation regarding alleged changes in Spain's immigration rules.

The incident also exposed diplomatic tensions between Spain and Morocco. Morocco does not recognize Madrid's claim to Ceuta, which has been under Spanish control for centuries. It remains to be seen how Rabat will react to Felipe's trip.

articles.headline: Super El Niño sets another record as it strengthens to 'unprecedented levels'
keyFacts: Australia's Bureau of Meteorology reported that sea-surface temperatures in the central Pacific have reached record levels.
Climate scientists describe the current El Niño event as unprecedented due to widespread ocean warmth exceeding previous historical records.
Forecasters expect the El Niño event to peak in December, likely contributing to record-breaking global temperatures through 2027.
body: - Published
El NiÃ±o has continued to strengthen to what some scientists are calling "unprecedented levels", weeks before its expected peak in December.
Several key measures are now in record territory.
In its latest update, Australia's Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) said average weekly sea-surface temperatures in the central Pacific have reached their highest level on record, external.

It comes after scientists declared a new record for daily sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern Pacific in September, exceeding the previous record set during the very strong El NiÃ±o of 2015.

Temperatures above 30C have also been recorded for the first time in parts of the tropical Pacific, while record sea-surface temperature anomalies and exceptional subsurface warmth have been observed.
These measurements come from the region of the equatorial Pacific used to monitor El NiÃ±o.
El NiÃ±o is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.
However, the Pacific is also warming due to human-induced climate change and this is starting to mask the strength of the natural warming during El NiÃ±o.
To remove this additional warming signal, Australian and US official forecasters are now using a Relative Ocean El NiÃ±o Index (RONI), to enable better comparison to historical events.
Using that measure, the BOM's average weekly data - while only going back to 2008 - is significant as it now exceeds levels during the record-breaking December of 2015.
"We are currently witnessing an El NiÃ±o event that is unprecedented in the historical record," Dr Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth, told the BBC.
Strong El NiÃ±o in a warmer world
The warmth across the Pacific now extends well beyond the tropical region normally used to monitor El NiÃ±o.
Comparisons with previous major events in 1972-73, 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 show much more widespread ocean warmth across the Pacific and into the Gulf of Mexico.
Part of this reflects the long-term warming of the oceans but scientists say it is not the whole story.
"The strength of El NiÃ±o this year is spilling out of the traditional El NiÃ±o region," Dr Hausfather said.

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says there is currently no evidence that climate change is making El NiÃ±o events stronger or more frequent, external. However, it remains an active area of scientific research.
What is clearer is that El NiÃ±o releases additional heat from the oceans into the atmosphere.
Historically, global temperatures during El NiÃ±o years are typically higher than during neutral years.
Combined with human-driven climate change, that extra heat is expected to help make 2026 one of the warmest years on record, with unusually high global temperatures likely to continue into 2027.
No two El NiÃ±o events are exactly alike
Although the most widespread impacts are expected later this year and into 2027, El NiÃ±o's influence is already being felt across parts of the world.
The strength of an El NiÃ±o does not automatically determine the scale of impacts in any one location. Regional effects can vary considerably from one event to another.
However, some common patterns are emerging when compared with previous super El NiÃ±os.
During the 1997-98 event, severe drought across south-east Asia contributed to extensive peat and forest fires, while parts of East Africa experienced devastating floods.
The event also helped make 1998 the warmest year on record at the time.
A similar pattern developed during the 2015-16 El NiÃ±o.
Severe drought and wildfire activity returned to parts of south-east Asia, while southern Africa experienced one of its worst droughts in decades, triggering a major humanitarian crisis.

Another recurring signal is tropical cyclone activity. Strong El NiÃ±o events typically suppress Atlantic hurricanes while boosting activity across parts of the Pacific, a pattern that has also been observed during 2026.

The World Meteorological Organisation says drought and flood-related disruption is already being reported in several regions, with growing concerns over food security in parts of East Africa and the Asia-Pacific.
Forecasts from both the European Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasts and the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration indicate El NiÃ±o is likely to peak in December.
Dr Hausfather said the latest projections were "astonishing" and are likely to set new records "by a remarkable amount".

articles.headline: '123456' password linked to Denmark data breach affecting 8.8M people
keyFacts: A data breach of Denmark's Central Register of Persons exposed the information of 8.8 million people.
An attacker reportedly gained access to the system using the weak password 123456 on a company account.
The breach was discovered after a government staffer noticed an invoice for unusually high system activity.
body: A person claiming responsibility for the breach of Denmark's Central Register of Persons (CPR) says they gained access through an IT company's account protected by the password "123456." The person told Danish news outlet Politiken they had no intention of selling or leaking the data. The newspaper reported that at least three company accounts, including an administrator account, used the same password. Denmark's CPR administration confirmed a breach affecting the information belonging to 8.8 million people on October 5, adding that a Danish company's legal access to the CPR system was abused. It did not name Funen-based Pays ApS as the company in question, but managing director Sophie Laursen confirmed on October 9 that it's access had been exploited. Pays' website has been taken offline, and the business has not responded to The Register's request for more information about the password claims. Pays had authorized access to the CPR system to provide services such as validating business customers' records. The Danish government says information relating to 8.8 million people was accessed. The register contains approximately 11 million records, including those of deceased people and people who have moved abroad. The government did not respond to questions about the alleged password failings. According to documents obtained by broadcaster TV 2, the attacker gained access to the CPR system on September 10 and ran the 14 million automated searches between then and September 20. The intrusion was detected on October 2, 12 days after the last reported searches. Mikkel Leihardt, director of the government's higher education and science ministry, told reporters at a press conference that the attack was discovered after a department staffer picked up an invoice indicating unusually high activity from Pays. The Danish data protection authority, Datatilsynet, was notified on October 4, and the government disclosed the attack the following day. ®

keyFacts: An NPR analysis found the federal government spent nearly $22 million in taxpayer funds on advertisements promoting Donald Trump.
Federal agents searched Representative Ilhan Omar's home in an ongoing investigation that she claimed was politically motivated by the Trump administration.
Donald Trump is traveling to Alaska today with more campaign events planned for later this week after holding an Ohio rally.
body: Government spent millions on Trump ads. And, federal agents raid Ilhan Omar's home
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories

The U.S. government continues to pay for ads promoting President Trump, even after he announced that his MAGA Inc. super PAC would take over funding. A federal judge ordered the ads to be taken down, yet they remained on air. An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer funds have been spent since the campaign began in late September. Almost $10 million of that was spent after Trump pledged on an Oct. 5 Truth Social post to fund the campaign privately. The White House has called the ads public service announcements, but a lawsuit by Common Cause and others argued they were funded without congressional approval, violating restrictions on taxpayer-funded publicity and propaganda.

Trump has ramped up his campaign travel ahead of the midterm elections. He rallied supporters in Youngstown, Ohio, last night and is heading to Alaska today. More events are planned for later this week. He has been trying to encourage his supporters to vote by telling them to pretend he is on the ballot.

- 🎧 Trump's events resemble his presidential campaign rallies: He emphasizes his accomplishments while calling out superfans and insulting Democrats, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First. Kurtzleben adds that Trump's campaign trail emphasizes that the GOP is still his party, despite his declining approval. Candidates like Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and GOP Sen. Jon Husted saw large, appreciative, but Kurtzleben says the benefits of appearing alongside Trump remain unclear.
- ➡️ With just weeks until Election Day, polls may start to flood the landscape. While they serve as a helpful tool, remember they can't predict the future. Keep these tips in mind as polls pour in.

- ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in Washington, D.C., yesterday morning. Omar, D-Minn., says the search was politically motivated by the Trump administration. The Department of Justice told NPR in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant," approved by the DOJ, as part of an ongoing federal investigation. Current and former federal officials with knowledge of the search who were not authorized to speak publicly confirmed the details, revealing that this multi-year probe includes whistleblower complaints and focuses on allegations of immigration fraud.

- 🎧 One of Omar's neighbors, 79-year-old Sharon Jackson, tells NPR's Luke Garrett she was awoken yesterday at around 4:30 a.m. by loud knocking and that vans and agents wearing gloves were walking to and from the congresswoman's house. Vice President JD Vance previously accused Omar of immigration fraud, which she denies. Omar is an American citizen who left Somalia as a refugee. She stated on social media that the president has spent a decade targeting her with smear campaigns and vowed not to be silenced. Trump says that he is not involved in the investigation into Omar.
Living better
Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles resurgence in decades. More than 3,600 confirmed cases and two deaths have been reported as of late September. Outbreaks in several states and exposures in public places like bars, sports stadiums and public transit have raised concerns about travel safety. Almost all U.S. measles cases involve unvaccinated individuals, and as the outbreaks grow in some states, the risk of exposure is getting higher. Here's what to know before traveling by plane or train.
- ✈️ People who've had two doses of the MMR vaccine are considered protected against measles.
- ✈️ The disease is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, breathes or sneezes. That airspace can remain contaminated for up to two hours.
- ✈️ Check with your healthcare provider about your vaccination status. They may recommend a booster based on your medical history and health.
- ✈️ Immunocompromised individuals may be unable to receive vaccination and often rely on herd immunity for protection. For measles, the vaccination threshold for herd immunity is 95%.
- ✈️ Measles can be hard to track because symptoms — such as fever, cough, and rash — typically appear seven to 14 days after exposure and can sometimes take long as 21 days to surface.
Picture show

The Metropolitan Museum of Art's new blockbuster exhibition showcases the works of two 20th-century artists. Jackson Pollock is well-known for his drip paintings. His wife, Lee Krasner, has often been overshadowed by her husband. This show finally gives Krasner the recognition she deserves. With more than 120 pieces on display — 74 from Krasner and 48 from Pollock — the show highlights Krasner as a titan of Abstract Expressionism, too. Check out some of the photos from the exhibit.
3 things to know before you go

- Americans Robert Hall from Stanford University and Michael Woodford from Columbia University have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on managing boom-and-bust cycles to reduce inflation and unemployment.
- Trump's new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, will hold her first press briefing today. She has raised her profile by appearing on conservative outlets and promoting right-wing conspiracy theories.

- Hectic early-morning traffic can make breakfast a luxury in Lagos, Nigeria. Akara is a roadside staple. For NPR's Breakfast Around the World series, Emmanuel Akinwotu explores the savory snack's deep roots in Nigeria and West Africa, and its spread around the world during the trans-Atlantic slave trade.
