articles.headline: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Reviews Hail a Triumphant Return
keyFacts: Konami released Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, the first mainline installment in the series in over a decade, developed by the studio Evil Empire.
The game has received strong reviews, with critics praising its combat and modernization while some questioned if it retains the series' classic spirit.
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse will be released on October 15 for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X.
body: If you haven't noticed, Konami is back, and the once-great Japanese publisher is finding its feet again by farming its properties out to hungry younger developers all over the world. This has worked pretty well for Silent Hill, and now it's Castlevania's turn with Castlevania: Belmont's Curse. The first mainline installment in the vampire action series in over 10 years, Belmont's Curse was made by Dead Cells support studio Evil Empire. (The groundwork for this collaboration was laid with the 2023 mashup Dead Cells: Return to Castlevania.)

It looks like Konami's strategy has worked again. Castlevania: Belmont's Curse has strong reviews, the majority hailing it as a triumphant return for, and smart modernization of, the series. But some critics query whether it has really captured the Castlevania spirit. Currently, the game's average rating on the review aggregation sites sits at 86 on Metacritic and 85 on OpenCritic.
Some critics say Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a 10/10

Leading the cheering squad is GameSpot's Steve Watts, who called Belmont's Curse "one of the best Castlevania games, and one of the best metroidvania games, of all time" in a 10/10 review. Watts hailed the "sprawling map bursting with mysteries to uncover, joyous traversal tools that make roaming the map feel great, a story that balances a macabre tone with occasional lightness, a cast of creative and well-drawn characters, and hands-down the best combat of any Castlevania game — in fact, among the best combat of any 2D action game, period."

Like many other reviewers, IGN's Scott White liked the new hero, Rose Belmont, and was impressed by the sharp and responsive combat, but felt that the latter came at the expense of some of Castlevania's classic characteristics, including the RPG system, and its unique feel. "So much else of what usually sets this series apart within this genre has been smoothed over with Belmont’s Curse, which leaves the whole package feeling a bit like a really solid metroidvania wearing a superficial Castlevania skin," White wrote. "There isn’t even a dagger to throw, which just feels kind of wrong. [Rose] doesn’t even start the game with a whip."

This wasn't a problem for Game Informer's Charles Harte, who noted that Belmont's Curse, while technically a sequel to Castlevania 3, follows on from the first two seasons of Netflix's Castlevania anime. "Arguably, it's a better sequel to the show than the game; the art style and character designs have clear anime inspirations, and many voice actors, including Trevor Belmont, reprise their roles," Harte said in a glowing 9.25/10 review. Harte also loved the new tarot card system, which unlocks upgradeable spells and also inspires some of the biggest treasure-hunts in the game.

Like IGN's White, The Guardian's Harper Jay MacIntyre noted a shift toward "twitch-based action" in Belmont's Curse and said it "may annoy purists, but you can't call it dull." MacIntyre's three-star review criticizes the focus on Super Meat Boy-style platforming gauntlets over puzzle-solving, and some uneven pacing. "This may be the most virtually striking Castlevania since 2002’s Harmony of Dissonance and sometimes it’s also the most inventive and brain-teasing," MacIntyre wrote. "In other moments, you’ll be bored to bloody tears."

But taken on its own merits, Belmont's Curse is "a near-perfect Metroidvania," according to Polygon's own Elijah Gonzalez. "By combining throwback appeal with razor-sharp gameplay built on the brilliant Dead Cells, Evil Empire’s latest lives up to Castlevania’s legendary status. From its bold use of color that makes the gothic visuals pop, to a new card-based Arcana system, Belmont’s Curse breathes new life into these games while honing in on what makes this series special."
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse will be released on Oct. 15 for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X.

articles.headline: Manchester City v PSG is a reminder of the path not taken in sanctions battles
keyFacts: Manchester City and Paris Saint-Germain were both found to have violated Uefa financial fair play rules in 2014.
A Premier League commission recently found Manchester City significantly breached spending limits and misstated accounts between 2009 and 2018.
Manchester City has appealed the Premier League commission's verdict while Paris Saint-Germain continues to deny any wrongdoing regarding financial regulations.
body: Nasser al-Khelaifi was among those unhappy with the timing of the release of Manchester City’s guilty verdict by the Premier League a fortnight ago, although his visit with Paris Saint-Germain to the Etihad Stadium for a Champions League game on Wednesday provides a timely reminder that it could have been far worse.

The two clubs are linked by more than their ownership by Gulf states, being among the first found to have broken Uefa’s financial fair play rules in 2014, and by a magnitude that would make subsequent offenders pale in comparison.

Uefa’s investigators found that between 2011 and 2013, when the maximum permitted loss for clubs competing in European competitions was €45m (£38m), PSG’s deficit was €218m and City’s €188m, yet both clubs avoided charges by signing settlement agreements.

With hindsight the terms seem generous to say the least, with sanctions limited to a financial penalty of €20m each, plus more onerous restrictions on their spending in subsequent years. City and PSG were made liable to pay a further €40m if they broke the terms of their settlements.

Uefa said in April 2017 that both clubs had “fully complied with all the requirements” but it remains an issue of contention whether City stuck to those spending limits. In 2020, after an investigation by Uefa’s investigatory chamber, the club was suspended from the Champions League for two years for “overstating its sponsorship revenue” between 2012 and 2016, before this was overturned by an appeal to the court of arbitration for sport, which found: “Most of the alleged breaches were either not established or time-barred.”

Then, last month, the Premier League announced that an independent commission convened to examine more than 100 charges against City had found that between seasons 2009-10 and 2017-18 the club was “significantly in breach” of Uefa’s spending limits and had “filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances”. City have appealed against the commission’s verdict.

PSG, where al-Khelaifi has been the president and face of the Qatari ownership since 2011, were fined a further €10m by Uefa in 2022 for not complying with financial rules since 2018, with another €50m suspended.

Part of al-Khelaifi’s annoyance at the Premier League last month stemmed from the fact that the release of the independent commission’s core judgment on City overshadowed the general assembly of European Football Clubs in Copenhagen, including his keynote speech, which featured City’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano, sitting in the front row before scurrying away from television cameras.

In his speech as EFC’s chair, al-Khelaifi outlined his plans to make it a global organisation and aimed some barbs at Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, over the importance of good governance, a far cry from his attitude towards Infantino a decade ago.

A 2018 investigation from the German publication Der Spiegel claimed that Infantino, then Uefa’s general secretary, had played a key role in ensuring PSG and City avoided more severe sanctions in 2014, including meeting with officials from both clubs for “secret talks, even supplying them with confidential materials” that involved suggested “compromises that he was unauthorised to propose”.

Der Spiegel also published an email from Infantino to City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, sent on 2 May 2014 in which he outlined the terms of a proposed settlement. “You will see that I’ve sometimes chosen a wording which ‘looks’ more ‘strong,’” Infantino wrote. “Please read the document with this spirit.”

Settlements with both clubs were agreed that month, although not before the head of Uefa’s investigatory chamber Brian Quinn, a former senior official at the Bank of England, resigned amid reports he considered the agreements too lenient.

“In cases where clubs overspend and balance their books only thanks to money injections, a settlement agreement has always been the preferred solution,” Uefa said at the time. “In such cases, the focus is on limiting the revenues coming from outside football.”

Infantino said his “job entails having discussions, having conversations, exchanging documents, drafts, ideas” and that he had been carrying out his duties “in an honest way, in a professional way and trying to defend the interests of football”.

PSG insist they have “always acted in full compliance with the laws and regulations enacted by sports institutions” and City’s protestations of innocence are well established, but the clubs now find themselves on different sides of the divide.

Whereas al-Khelaifi will arrive in Manchester as the face of the establishment, with EFC joint shareholders with Uefa in the commercial company that runs the Champions League, City remain the insurgents, continuing to rage against the machine.

Many City fans will continue to show their disdain for Uefa by booing the Champions League anthem, but some may be quietly wondering whether their Abu Dhabi leadership could have followed the more diplomatic path taken by PSG.

articles.headline: Katie Zacharia steps into White House spotlight as Trump faces midterm headwinds
keyFacts: Katie Zacharia will hold her first briefing as the new White House press secretary on Tuesday, succeeding Karoline Leavitt.
Zacharia takes office three weeks before the midterm elections as Republicans face the prospect of losing their congressional majorities.
Congressional Democrats are signaling plans to investigate the administration and potentially seek a third impeachment if they regain majorities.
body: Katie Zacharia will hold her first briefing as the new White House press secretary Tuesday morning, exactly three weeks — and roughly twelve hours — before polls close in the 2026 midterm elections .

Zacharia takes over at a precarious political moment for President Donald Trump , with Republicans facing the prospect of losing their congressional majorities and the White House looking to sharpen its messaging ahead of Election Day. She also faces the challenge of succeeding Karoline Leavitt , who established herself as both a capable manager and a formidable public advocate for the president.

Leavitt was the youngest person ever in that position, and she quickly developed a reputation last year for not only being a bulldog on the airwaves, where she deftly defended the totality of Trump’s policy agenda, but also seamlessly running the White House’s messaging apparatus.

Leavitt also reshaped the White House press corps, taking back moderation of the protective pool from the White House Correspondents’ Association and opening up the corps to “new media” outlets and reporters, many of whom lend the president favorable coverage compared with legacy media outlets.
As one former senior White House official put it, Leavitt’s tenure was a “night and day” difference compared with her immediate predecessor, Karine Jean Pierre.

Zacharia, meanwhile, arrives with a different resume and a less established record managing a major communications operation, though she shares Leavitt’s reputation as a staunch defender of the president on television.

A trained attorney, she spent three years working in Beijing, including time with the World Bank, and most immediately served as a senior communications adviser for Trump Media Group, which operates Trump’s Truth Social.

Zacharia’s sole government experience is a college internship during the George W. Bush administration and a brief stint as a communications aide at the Department of Homeland Security. Zacharia spent several weeks this year working as assistant secretary for public affairs under former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem.

Since Trump reentered office, Zacharia has most notably been a staunchly loyal television surrogate, which people familiar with the hiring say made her a top press secretary candidate in the president’s eyes.

Trumpworld insiders previously told the Washington Examiner that, after Leavitt’s exit, Trump wanted to remake the entire White House messaging apparatus, prioritizing an incoming press secretary’s on-air appearances over the behind-the-scenes managerial aspects of the position.

“The president is his own best spokesman,” one veteran GOP operative who works closely with the president’s outside political operation explained. “So why does he even need a press secretary? Well, he needs more allies on TV, defending the administration from a hostile press and framing wins for downballot Republican candidates, to point to. Katie is the perfect fit.”

“Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team,” added White House communications director Steven Cheung. “She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary.”

Zacharia’s ability to make the case for Trump’s agenda could face an immediate test as Republicans confront an increasingly difficult political environment in the final weeks before the midterm elections.

Polls show the war in Iran, elevated prices, and a host of other issues are driving down enthusiasm among GOP voters heading into November. As of Monday, Trump’s approval rating in the RealClearPolitics polling average was more than 21 points underwater, with just 38.1% approval.

Meanwhile, Democrats hold a more than 8-point polling advantage over Republicans on generic House ballots, in addition to leads in the Senate races in Alaska, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas. Iowa and Kansas, both traditionally viewed as Republican strongholds, are virtually tied. If Democrats flip four Senate seats, they will retake the majority in the upper chamber.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance are spending the final weeks of the cycle crisscrossing the country campaigning for Republicans, but losing the GOP majority in the Senate would make governing particularly difficult. A Democratic majority would have enhanced leverage to block administration and judicial nominations across Trump’s final two years in office.
ROB CRILLY | SEVEN TV HITS A DAY AND A CRUCIAL ALLY: HOW KATIE ZACHARIA CAUGHT TRUMP’S EYE

Furthermore, congressional Democrats are already signaling that they plan to use those majorities to investigate senior members of the Trump administration, probe the business dealings of the president’s family, and, potentially, seek a third impeachment of Trump himself.

articles.headline: Two US cities could soon ban one of the world’s most controversial foods
keyFacts: Voters in Washington, DC, and Denver will decide in November whether to ban foie gras sales in restaurants and grocery stores.
Animal advocacy groups launched the measures, arguing that force-feeding ducks to enlarge their livers is uniquely cruel.
Producers and chefs argue foie gras is unfairly singled out, but researchers reported force-feeding causes injuries and impaired mobility.
body: An employee holds fatty duck liver — or foie gras — at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York. | Pro-Animal Future

In November, voters in Washington, DC, and Denver will cast their ballots to decide whether their cities’ restaurants and grocery stores can continue to sell one of the world’s more controversial foods: foie gras.

French for “fatty liver,” foie gras is made by briefly force-feeding ducks a corn slurry two to three times daily with a metal tube during the final two to three weeks of their lives. It can make their livers balloon to roughly six to 10 times their natural size.

The farming practice gives the liver its signature rich, buttery taste that made it a French delicacy centuries ago and ever since, a prized menu item at upscale restaurants, particularly in Europe, the United States, and East Asia. But the apparent cruelty of force-feeding ducks has also long made it the target of those concerned with animal welfare.

While forcing a lot of food through a metal tube into ducks’ throats may not look great, foie gras companies and high-end chefs contend that it doesn’t hurt the animals because — among other reasons — ducks’ unique physiology enables them to eat fish and other animals whole, and that they naturally gorge before migrations. (More on these arguments later).

Whenever the issue is up for a vote, it touches off fierce debates over animal welfare and fine dining. While foie gras production does harm animals, producers and chefs maintain the dish is unfairly singled out when there are arguably worse practices in animal agriculture, including many that impact a far greater number of animals . Banning a product largely consumed by the 1 percent might make some voters feel good, while ignoring the animal cruelty embedded in the production of vastly more common products, like chicken and eggs .

But to animal rights advocates, a potential ban in DC — which has more foie gras-serving restaurants than almost anywhere else in the US — represents a unique opportunity to hasten the end of what spokesperson Natalie Fulton of Pro-Animal DC , the group behind the DC ballot measure, calls a “uniquely cruel” practice.
What the science says about force-feeding ducks

Foie gras producers often argue that ducks can handle force-feeding just fine because of their long, flexible necks that allow them to swallow fish whole — spines and all — and that they’ve evolved to stuff themselves before seasonal migrations. Producers also commonly say that they have no gag reflex.

But these claims, according to research, don’t mean that force-feeding is painless. They also leave out a lot of the other problems in foie gras production. Last month, a veterinarian at Ghent University in Belgium and a team of animal welfare research consultants published a literature review in the journal Animals looking at how foie gras farming affects ducks .

For one, there’s a big difference between ducks swallowing fish and having a rigid metal tube inserted into their throat dozens of times. A duck’s throat and beak area are particularly sensitive, and repeated insertion can cause tissue damage and irritation and inflammation in their esophagus, according to the newly published research, which was funded by the Flemish government. And while wild waterfowl might gorge before migrations, the resulting liver enlargement in the wild doesn’t come anywhere near what it does on foie gras farms.

Beyond the arguments as to whether ducks can be humanely force-fed, there are plenty of other welfare concerns in foie gras production. Eating so much makes the ducks overweight, which makes it harder for them to move around. Liver enlargement increases their internal heat production, which can make ducks pant more, and an enlarged liver can put pressure on their air sacs, also making it harder to breathe.

“The available evidence indicates that force-feeding creates substantial risks of welfare compromise through repeated restraint and tube insertion, possible injuries to the upper digestive tract, progressive liver enlargement, altered hepatic [liver] function, increased metabolic heat load, and impaired mobility,” the researchers concluded.

Ducks raised for foie gras aren’t given access to water — like a pond or bathing trough — which in nature they use to clean themselves and forage. And the overwhelming majority of those reared in the US even lack access to the outdoors.

Despite some of the documented welfare concerns in foie gras farming, Jordan Ginor — a director at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York — told me that they’ve got “really good, clean, smiley, healthy ducks.” The company is one of the two main commercial foie gras producers in the US and raises hundreds of thousands of ducks for foie gras annually.

Ginor also said that the aforementioned literature review focuses on European foie gras production, where birds are typically force-fed larger meals, twice daily, over two weeks. But at Hudson Valleys Farms, he said, the process is slower: smaller meals, thrice daily, over three weeks. “The slow process, with significantly less food per meal, lessens any possibility of stress or negative impacts,” he said. (Though one could argue that more insertions over a longer period is worse for the ducks.)

Earlier this year, a photojournalist who took a public tour of Hudson Valley Farms documented — during the force-feeding phase — ducks confined in small pens with no bedding. In one part of the video, the ducks gather in the corner of the pen, seemingly in a fruitless attempt to escape force-feeding.

When I asked Ginor for a response to the video, he was dismissive of the investigations into his company. “We’re proud of what we do,” he said. “Anyone’s welcome to go in and see.” (To its credit, the company provides free public tours, which is highly unusual for large-scale meat producers.)

In previous investigations of the company , animal advocates alleged they documented ducks injured, lame, bloodied, heavily panting, overcrowded in large barns, and confined in small cages prior to slaughter.

The other main commercial US farm, La Belle Farm, also in upstate New York, did not respond to an interview request for this story. La Belle has received far less attention than Hudson Valley Farms, though a 2019 news story found that its housing and practices are similar to those of its counterpart.
Why single out foie gras?
Support for a foie gras ban neared 80 percent in a small 2023 poll of Washington, DC, residents, with similar support in a 2026 Denver poll .
“We’ve tried to diversify, given everything that’s been going on” with foie gras bans over the last 20-odd years, Ginor told me. But foie gras is still the core of Hudson Valley Farms’ business.

Ginor said his operation is more humane than a lot of other poultry farms, so why single out foie gras? “As soon as we start comparing how things work at other farms, we look much more favorably,” he told me.

He may have a point, though it’d be difficult to crunch the moral math and determine whether foie gras is much worse — or perhaps even not as bad — as the factory farming of America’s chickens, egg-laying hens , and turkeys . Around half of US egg-laying hens live in tiny cages, while turkeys and chickens raised for meat have been bred to grow so big and fast that they have difficulty walking. And they all outnumber foie gras ducks by many orders of magnitude.

I asked Fulton of Pro-Animal DC about singling out foie gras over other issues. “Just because some things are also bad doesn’t mean that foie gras production is good,” she told me. (Pro-Animal Future, its umbrella group, is also behind the Denver ballot measure .)

Much of the issue boils down to what’s politically possible. While there’s been some progress, it’s proven difficult and expensive for animal advocates to reform poultry farming in state legislatures. Foie gras, on the other hand, is sort of a low-hanging fruit; there isn’t a large lobby group behind the US industry, and since it’s a luxury product, most consumers won’t miss it.

And Denver and DC are just the latest in a string of fights over foie gras. Its sale has been banned in California, along with Portland, Oregon; Pittsburgh, and New York City, whose ban has been held up in court in recent years. Over the summer, Brazil banned the sale and production of foie gras, too, and around 20 other countries — mostly in Europe — prohibit its production. (Chicago’s 2006 ban was overturned two years later.)
“We have no money to fight the story,” Ginor said. “People want to attack the 1 percent luxury food.”
Bart Hutchins, head chef at Butterworth’s in Washington, DC, told me he doesn’t want his town to ban what he considers a “great culinary tradition.”

“It is a miracle that we discovered this and that we cultivated it and that we can eat it,” he told me. For his part, Hutchins would rather see animal rights activists work to improve farming conditions for animals farmed on a much larger scale, like chickens and pigs, rather than ban one niche ingredient.

But he may soon have to take foie gras off his menu. Pro-Animal Future is especially confident about DC voters’ support for the ban, which would be a blow to the small US foie gras industry. But another incremental step in advancing animal welfare — and the issue in the minds of more voters.

articles.headline: US soldiers can't be protected from all bioweapons, Army admits amid troubling surge in threats
keyFacts: The U.S. Army launched a new plan to train soldiers to fight through biological attacks rather than assuming all threats can be stopped.
Army official Dr. Alison Tamasi stated that the military cannot protect every soldier from every possible biological threat.
The Army aims to prepare forces to operate in biologically contested environments by 2035 by integrating biological incident scenarios into routine combat training.
body: The U.S. Army unveiled its plan to prepare soldiers to fight through biological attacks rather than assume every threat can be stopped.

The newly signed plan bringing biological warfare scenarios into routine combat training as artificial intelligence (AI) and biotechnology raise new concerns about the weapons America's adversaries could develop in the near future.

"Can we protect every soldier from every possible bio threat? Probably not," Dr. Alison Tamasi, a senior official at the Army's Nuclear and Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction Agency, told reporters on Monday.
"We can't put them in a bubble," she added.

The shift comes as U.S. officials continue to assess whether Moscow maintains an offensive biological weapons program after a mysterious death in Russia was linked to an anti-plague facility — reviving questions of biological safety and transparency.
CHINESE AI MODEL INVESTIGATED AFTER RESEARCHER SAYS IT PROVIDED INSTRUCTIONS FOR BIOWEAPONS, ASSASSINATIONS
Still, the Army hopes their implemented plan will help prepare the force to deploy and fight in biologically contested environments by 2035.

Rather than treating outbreaks primarily as medical emergencies, the military wants commanders, intelligence officers and logistics personnel to prepare for biological threats while continuing to carry out their combat missions.
EMERGING TECH HAS NEW ARMY LEADERS WARNING TROOPS CAN'T ‘AI’ THEIR WAY TO VICTORY ON THE BATTLEFIELD
One of the biggest changes will be bringing biological incidents into major Army combat exercises , forcing commanders to respond to potential outbreaks while continuing their other missions.
Rather than relying on specialized biological exercises, the Army wants troops across different military functions to confront biological threats as part of their regular training.

Tamasi described one scenario involving a simulated norovirus outbreak at a military port. While medical personnel worked to contain the outbreak, logistics officers would have to determine how to keep critical supplies moving.

The example illustrates a broader shift in the Army's approach: Biological threats are no longer being treated solely as medical problems but as potential disruptions to military operations that commanders must be prepared to manage.
"We need to make sure that doctrine is aligned," Tamasi said, explaining that the Army is working to establish how biodefense readiness should be assessed across the force.

The new plan, signed last week, puts into motion the Army's updated biodefense strategy released in September, which sets a goal of preparing soldiers to deploy and fight in biologically contested environments by 2035.

The first two-year implementation cycle will focus on establishing policies, improving coordination across Army organizations and developing personnel with specialized biological expertise. More advanced technologies and acquisition efforts are expected in later phases.
The effort comes amid growing concerns about the potential for artificial intelligence and biotechnology to accelerate the development of biological threats.
PLAGUE MYSTERY REVIVES CONCERNS OVER NOT-TO-SECRET RUSSIAN BIOWEAPONS PROGRAM
Tamasi described those advances as a dual-use challenge, with technologies that can accelerate medical discoveries also potentially enabling new biological threats to emerge more quickly.

Russia remains a particular concern for U.S. national security officials. Washington has long assessed that Moscow maintains an offensive biological weapons program inherited from the Soviet Union, despite Russia's obligations under the Biological Weapons Convention.
The United States renounced offensive biological weapons in 1969 and is also a party to the convention, which prohibits the development, production and stockpiling of biological weapons.
US, WHO REQUEST DETAILS FROM RUSSIA AMID REPORTS OF SECOND PNEUMONIA CASE

Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, died Oct. 2 after developing severe pneumonia. Russian media initially reported a possible pneumonic plague infection following a suspected laboratory accident, but Russian authorities denied that an accident occurred and said testing found no evidence of plague or other high-threat pathogens.

The cause of her death remains undetermined. In an Oct. 10 update, the World Health Organization said it had found no evidence of ongoing transmission linked to the case, while noting that a confirmed diagnosis was still lacking.
Asked how much Russia's biological weapons activities informed the Army's planning, Tamasi said the strategy was based on "intelligence writ large" rather than any single adversary.
"It's not solely focused on a particular threat actor," she said.

Asked what lessons the Army had drawn from Russia's biological weapons program, Tamasi said the strategy was designed to address biological threats regardless of their origin — whether accidental, deliberate or ultimately determined not to pose the threat initially feared.

For Army commanders, she explained, the immediate priority is responding to a potential biological threat and maintaining operations, rather than determining its origin. Questions of attribution would involve the broader U.S. government.
That approach also informs how the Army intends to detect emerging threats.
Officials said the military is working to draw together information from environmental monitoring, medical facilities and intelligence reporting to identify potential biological incidents earlier.

That could include wastewater surveillance similar to monitoring used during the COVID-19 pandemic , Tamasi said. The goal is to give commanders a more complete picture of potential biological threats so they can respond before disruptions spread.

The COVID-19 pandemic also exposed the limitations of treating biological threats primarily as public health emergencies, according to Army officials, reinforcing the need for military leaders outside the medical field to incorporate those risks into operational planning.

The strategy addresses misinformation as another operational challenge, particularly when troops and commanders must make decisions about vaccines , protective measures and communications during a biological incident.

The Army has also begun rolling out biodefense seminars for senior leaders. Tamasi said one three-star board determined that senior Army leaders should receive at least an hour of instruction on biodefense and the "ground truth" surrounding biological threats.
Ultimately, the Army hopes that preparing soldiers to continue their missions despite a biological attack could also discourage adversaries from using such weapons in the first place.
Tamasi said demonstrating that biological threats would not necessarily stop American forces from fighting could reduce the military advantage an adversary might hope to gain from deploying them.

articles.headline: Asha Sharma reportedly tells rattled Xbox employees: "We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP"
keyFacts: Xbox leader Asha Sharma reportedly told employees that the company must create new intellectual property to survive rather than relying solely on past franchises.
Sharma made these comments during a recent company-wide town hall meeting while discussing the future of Xbox and its next-generation console project.
The reported focus on new ideas contrasts with recent studio closures and staff cuts at Microsoft's gaming division.
body: Xbox leader Asha Sharma has reportedly broadcast her intent to "create enduring new IP" alongside the company's much publicised plan to organise around its biggest gaming brands - think The Elder Scrolls, think Blizzard, etc. But according to Sharma: "We will not survive if we only revive on the past."

Sharma apparently made those comments during a company-wide 'town hall' meeting last week, which Windows Central claims to have seen transcripts of. Incidentally, we've asked Microsoft to verify this town hall meeting took place and whether these transcripts are accurate.
Sharma reportedly said this in addition to dropping more information about Xbox's next-gen console Project Helix and while reflecting on Xbox's "return to growth" after "an all-time low".

"We're backing our strongest franchises," Sharma allegedly said. "I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises. I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP. We will not survive if we only revive on the past. We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences."

It's a declaration which seems at odds with Xbox's recent actions. Parting ways with studios like Double Fine and Compulsion, and probably Arkane - all of which have a track record in creating new game ideas such as Keeper and South of Midnight, and Dishonored and Deathloop - seems an odd way to go about engendering a culture of courage in creation. Similarly, having an inventive studio like Obsidian work under Bethesda making a Fallout game suggests there's no immediate room there to pursue wholly original ideas. But at least Xbox is investing in Hideo Kojima's Physint, right? Right?

Cuts at id Software and consolidation elsewhere across the Xbox gaming division also reflect a company that appears to be reorganising around its biggest gaming brands rather than one intent on taking new, creative risks. Indeed, a look at Xbox's upcoming roster really only reveals InXile's Clockwork Revolution - one of its two Xbox exclusives - as an obvious contender in the 'big new idea' area. But will it be strong enough to start a lasting series?

Meanwhile, the studio behind the other Xbox exclusive, Gears of War: E-Day, fears for its future after releasing its game, despite it seeming to have been a success. That's because of the hundreds of impending cuts Microsoft still intends to make to its Xbox division. There, uncertainty looms large.

Dom reviewed Gears of War: E-Day for us recently and, generally, really enjoyed it. "Though there's still plenty of waist-high cover, ebb-and-flow firefighting, and braindead machismo, Gears E-Day proves that looking back can, indeed, help you look forward, too," Dom wrote.

articles.headline: Character.AI files for bankruptcy
keyFacts: Character.AI has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and is seeking to sell its assets to Disney.
Disney is the lead bidder for the company's assets, offering $20 million and hiring several members of the startup's technical team.
Character.AI expects to complete the sale process by late November or early December while continuing to operate its services.
body: Character.AI, one of the first breakout startups of the generative AI boom, has filed for bankruptcy and is selling some of its assets to Disney. The company, which builds various online bots for users to chat or roleplay with, has faced mounting scrutiny and lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, but has continued releasing updates and products in recent months.
Character.AI files for bankruptcy
The chatbot startup is looking to sell its assets to Disney after years of legal challenges and safety concerns.

In a press release and blog post published Monday, Character said it had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the US to facilitate the sale of the company and its assets. “Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds,” the company said.

In its bankruptcy filing, Character listed estimated liabilities between $50 million and $100 million. As part of the proposed sale, Disney would serve as the lead bidder for Character.AI’s assets, setting a baseline for competing offers. Disney would pay $20 million for certain undisclosed assets, and provide transition support “using former Company employees it has hired.” It would also receive a nonexclusive license to unspecified intellectual property.

Disney’s involvement comes shortly after the entertainment behemoth hired Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand as chief technology officer, part of its growing push into AI. Anand’s tenure as Character CEO lasted just over a year and during that time he oversaw the company’s move into microdramas. Disney has previously complained that Character was damaging its brand and exploiting its intellectual property by allowing unauthorized chatbots of its characters, including sending cease and desist letters.

Along with Anand, Disney also said it expected “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” to join the company. The move resembles a kind of “acquihire” strategy that has become increasingly common in Silicon Valley as a means of hoovering up startups’ talent that sometimes leaves the original company struggling to survive. Character.AI has survived it once already — Google spent over $2 billion to hire away much of the company’s talent, including co-founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, in 2024.

Character said it expects the sale process to be completed by late November or early December and plans to continue operating its services, including paid subscriptions, in the meantime. However, the company warned that “the platform will be wound down” if a suitable bid does not emerge. “As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging experience for our community remains a top priority,” it said.

articles.headline: Bethell returns as England call up youngsters Jack and Rew
keyFacts: Jacob Bethell returns to England's white-ball squad for the Australia tour following a knee injury.
Thomas Rew and Eddie Jack received their first international call-ups for the T20 series.
The tour begins with the first ODI in Perth on 13 November and concludes on 2 December.
body: - Published
Jacob Bethell will return for England's white-ball tour of Australia, while there are also first international call-ups for exciting prospects Thomas Rew and Eddie Jack.
Warwickshire's Bethell has not played since suffering a knee injury in July but is back as part of a near-full-strength squad for three one-day internationals.

England have made changes for the five T20s, resting players ahead of the Test tour of South Africa, meaning 18-year-old Somerset wicketkeeper-batter Rew and Hampshire's 21-year-old pace bowler Jack are included.

The tour begins with the first ODI in Perth on 13 November and ends with the final T20 in Canberra on 2 December â a week before England's warm-up match in South Africa leading into a three-Test series.
There will be live ball-by-ball commentary from every match of England's tour of Australia on Test Match Special.
England white-ball coach Brendon McCullum had previously confirmed he wanted a strong team for the ODI leg of the trip to Australia in the build-up to the World Cup in southern Africa next year.
The New Zealander also conceded he would have to rotate his squad for the T20 leg, given England's schedule in a busy winter of five separate overseas tours.

One-day squad: Harry Brook (Yorkshire â captain), Jofra Archer (Sussex), Gus Atkinson (Surrey), Sonny Baker (Hampshire), Tom Banton (Somerset), Jacob Bethell (Warwickshire), Jordan Cox (Essex), Henry Crocombe (Surrey), Sam Curran (Surrey), Liam Dawson (Hampshire), Ben Duckett (Nottinghamshire), Will Jacks (Surrey), Jamie Overton (Surrey), Adil Rashid (Yorkshire), Joe Root (Yorkshire), Josh Tongue (Nottinghamshire).

T20 squad: Harry Brook (Yorkshire â captain), Tom Banton (Somerset), Jacob Bethell (Warwickshire), James Coles (Sussex), Jordan Cox (Essex), Henry Crocombe (Surrey), Sam Curran (Surrey), Liam Dawson (Hampshire), Aneurin Donald (Derbyshire), Eddie Jack (Hampshire), Will Jacks (Surrey), Jamie Overton (Surrey), Adil Rashid (Yorkshire), Thomas Rew (Somerset), Phil Salt (Lancashire), Luke Wood (Lancashire).
âââââââââââââââââââ
Exciting Rew in line for history-making debut
For the ODIs, Jofra Archer is back in the pace attack after being rested for the tri-series in Pakistan in October.
Archer's return means the 50-over squad is close to full strength, bar the absence of wicketkeeper Jos Buttler who is set for a lengthy spell on the sidelines following hamstring surgery.
After the ODIs, all of seamers Archer, Gus Atkinson, Josh Tongue and Sonny Baker, along with batter Ben Duckett, miss out on the T20s in order to prepare for South Africa.
The re-shuffle means eye-catching call-ups for Rew and Jack, while opener Aneurin Donald keeps his place after making his debut in the series against Sri Lanka last month.

The addition of Rew and Jack, who were awarded development central contracts on Monday, offers the tantalising prospect of a first international cap against England's fiercest rivals in one of the most iconic venues in cricket. The first T20 is at the colossal Melbourne Cricket Ground on 21 November.

Rew does not turn 19 until 29 November. If he plays on the tour, he would become the third-youngest man to make his England debut in any format after Rehan Ahmed and Brian Close, and the youngest man to play for England against Australia.
Rew is the younger brother of James, who made his Test debut for England against New Zealand at The Oval in June.
Thomas captained England Under-19s to the final of the World Cup earlier this year and made two centuries for Somerset in the County Championship during the summer.
Jack, who has the middle name Vaughan after former England captain Michael, has been on England's radar since last year.

He looks likely to earn a debut in Australia because he is one of only three specialist fast bowlers in the squad. Uncapped Henry Crocombe is down under for both series after earning a two-year central contract on Monday, while Luke Wood is part of the T20 squad despite losing his central deal.
Bethell's return to both squads is an indication of the selection decision England will face for the Test series in South Africa.

In the left-hander's absence for the home Test series against Pakistan this summer, Emilio Gay, Jordan Cox and Dan Lawrence came into the England XI. Bethell's comeback could displace any one of that trio.

Harry Brook captains England on both legs of the tour and is once again set to play across formats in every game of the winter. He has not missed an international since a raft of players were rested for the T20 series in Ireland last September.
The trip will be Brook's first return to Australia since a nightclub incident in Wellington, New Zealand, last October was revealed on the final day of the Ashes series in January.

During the Ashes, England's players came under intense scrutiny from the local media, not helped by a series of off-field misdemeanours. Though a white-ball tour will not have the same profile as the Ashes, the tourists can still expect a degree of hostility from the home fans.
There will also be the spectre of former Test captain Ben Stokes, whose stint with Adelaide Strikers in the Big Bash League begins shortly after England's tour ends.

articles.headline: Phase Eight and Hobbs owner hit by cyber-attack, as H&M probes separate hack claim
keyFacts: TFG London is investigating a cyber-security incident that impacted IT systems for its Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles fashion brands.
TFG London stated it does not believe customer payment information was affected and will notify individuals if their personal data was compromised.
H&M is also investigating a separate claim that it was targeted by a hacking group, though it has found no evidence of a breach.
body: - Published
The owner of high-end fashion brands Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight says it is investigating a cyber-security incident.

According to TFG London - the UK arm of retail conglomerate The Foschini Group - it identified an incident on Sunday affecting some IT systems and "specifically impacting our Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles brands".
"We are actively investigating and working with external cyber security specialists," the company told BBC News in a statement.
Meanwhile, H&M is investigating a separate claim that it was attacked by a notorious hacking group.

TFG said its brands' stores are operating as normal but some website capabilities may be unavailable, adding "we apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate".
The retail group reportedly told customers in an email that it did not believe customers' payment information had been affected by the incident.
"As our investigation continues, we will be working to identify if any sensitive information related to our customers was impacted," it said.
The email, seen by news service PA, also said that those whose personal information had been impacted would be informed directly.
"We do not believe it is necessary to change your account login information at this time," it added.
Beverley Griffiths, senior lecturer in security and resilience at Bucks New University told PA that this was "a clear sign that major brands are firmly in the crosshairs of cyber attackers".
Fashion giants ranging from Adidas to Alexander McQueen have been targeted by cyber-criminals seeking to extort money by threatening to release customer data unless they are paid a ransom.

"No organisation is immune, so the real test of resilience is how quickly a business can detect an incident, respond and recover while keeping its customers informed," Griffiths said - adding customers should stay "vigilant" and wary of suspicious messages.

Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, said attacks targeting retailers were "starting to look rather like buses... you wait for one, and suddenly three come along at once".

She told the BBC that while it was too soon to ascertain how the incident affecting TFG London's systems occurred, or whether it was related to other recent hacks, "the retail industry has some serious questions to answer about how exposed its systems have become".
H&M investigating hack claim
On Monday, it was also reported that fashion giant H&M was investigating a claim of a hack by a cyber-criminal group called ShinyHunters.
The hackers have been previously linked to high-profile attacks including targeting the FBI, Rockstar Games and Ticketmaster.
"We are aware of information circulating online regarding a potential cyber security incident and are currently investigating the claims," H&M told BBC News in a statement.
"At this time, we have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised."
It also comes only a week after Asos customers were informed the online fashion and beauty retailer had been hacked by another group, via a push notification appearing on their phone screens.
Cyber-security experts told the BBC it was an unprecedented move for hackers to effectively transform an app notification system into a "ransom note".
It later emerged that hackers had obtained more detailed personal information belonging to Asos customers than the retailer initially suggested.

An update was issued to customers after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said the breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

articles.headline: Abdul El-Sayed’s alleged family ties to Muslim Brotherhood surface after denying any link during NBC interview
keyFacts: Abdul El-Sayed’s alleged family ties to Muslim Brotherhood surface after denying any link during NBC interview By Joseph A.

Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is facing new scrutiny after he denied that he or his family had any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.
body: Abdul El-Sayed’s alleged family ties to Muslim Brotherhood surface after denying any link during NBC interview
By
Joseph A. Wulfsohn, Fox News
Published Oct. 12, 2026, 11:54 p.m. PT

Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is facing new scrutiny after he denied that he or his family had any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.
On Sunday’s “Meet the Press,” NBC’s Kristen Welker pressed El-Sayed whether he could “set the record straight” on allegations that his family had connections to the controversial Islamist group.
“No,” El-Sayed replied.
“No, you don’t have any ties, and your family doesn’t?” Welker followed up.
“No,” El-Sayed repeated before suggesting his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, was floating Islamophobic attacks against him and his family.
However, according to his half-sister Eman Abdelhadi, their mother was an active member of the Muslim Brotherhood.

“Had an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college #respect,” Abdelhadi wrote in a 2012 X post, as first reported by the Washington Free Beacon.
Their mother, Fatten Elkomy, had attended Egypt’s Alexandria University, which, according to a report from the Brookings Institution, had strong Muslim Brotherhood activity back in the 70s.
In another 2012 post, Abdelhadi, a professor at the University of Chicago, wrote: “My family has long been MB, but I’ve always felt that it has navigated the political sphere poorly/destructively.”
In a third post from 2013, she wrote, “Praying for all my family that supports the #MB in #Egypt. Lie low, stay safe.”
An El-Sayed campaign spokesperson issued a statement to Fox News, saying, “Abdul is a dad and a doctor. He has spent his entire career working to keep Michiganders healthy and safe.

“Independent fact checkers have repeatedly debunked Mike’s lies, but their campaign continues to use bad faith attacks on Abdul’s faith and family. Mike wants to distract from Trump’s agenda that is terrorizing Michigan families at the pump and at the grocery store.”
The campaign has also said the Muslim Brotherhood accusations have been “debunked as racist and untrue.”
NBC News did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

articles.headline: Kristi Noem Tries Trolling Kacey Musgraves Over James Talarico, Receives A Brutal Reply
keyFacts: Kristi Noem criticized Kacey Musgraves on social media after the singer appeared in photos with Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico.
Musgraves responded to Noem by referencing the politician's admission in her memoir that she shot and killed her own dog.
Noem, currently serving as Donald Trump's Special Envoy for the Shield of the Americas, did not provide a further public response to the singer.
body: Country music star Kacey Musgraves had a doggone withering response after Kristi Noem tried to troll her over the Texas Senate race.

Noem, the former Department of Homeland Security secretary, took aim at Musgraves on Monday after Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico shared photos of himself with the Grammy-winning singer.
Noem pettily declared that she prefers country singer Ella Langley “over Kacey Musgraves any day.”
“And If I’m choosin’ Texas, I’ll take Ken Paxton over James Talarico,” she added, referencing Talarico’s controversy-engulfed Republican opponent in the 2026 midterm elections.

Musgraves, a Texas native herself who met Talarico at her performance at the American Airlines Center in Dallas on Saturday, didn’t let Noem’s dig lie and hit back with a one-liner about one of the most infamous controversies of her political career.
“I don’t think you have a dog in this fight but if you did you would have shot it,” Musgraves replied to Noem, who is now Donald Trump’s Special Envoy for the Shield of the Americas.
Musgraves was referring to Noem’s startling admission in her 2024 memoir, “No Going Back,” that she had shot and killed a dog named Cricket, her 14-month-old wire-haired pointer.
Noem wrote that Cricket had behaved aggressively and was difficult to train as a hunting dog, describing her as “less than worthless.”

articles.headline: Want Your New iPhone Duo Fast? Lock in Your Details Now
keyFacts: Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first foldable smartphone, during an event led by new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus.
The device features a 7.6-inch folding display and ranges from $1,999 to $3,199, making it Apple's most expensive iPhone.
Shoppers can save their purchase details on Apple's staging page before official preorders open at 5 a.m. PT on Friday.
body: If you’re eager to get your hands on the highly anticipated iPhone Duo, the first foldable iPhone, here’s how to get a head start on ordering. Apple has opened a staging page for preorders on apple.com, where you can get ready to place a preorder for the viral phone.

Head over to Apple’s online storefront, and you’ll find that a new iPhone Duo configurator is now live. On that page, save your preferred phone color, storage, mobile carrier and payment method. Saving these details in advance ensures you can complete your purchase immediately when preorders open at 5 a.m. PT on Friday.

Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo, one of its first new products under the helm of new CEO John Ternus, during its Surprise and Shine event in Cupertino, California, on Friday. It’s the first foldable from Apple, although merely the latest in a wave of new bendy phones to hit the market.

The iPhone Duo opens to reveal a 7.6-inch display and folds down to a pocketable passport size. The shifting shape supports split-screen multitasking and Apple Pencil, and brings a host of new features and animations to Apple iOS 27.

Pricing starts at $1,999 for the 512GB model and tops out at $3,199 for the 2TB version — before carrier subsidies — making the iPhone Duo the most expensive iPhone ever released. Price aside, observers expect demand among early adopters to be high, so prepping your order now is a smart idea.

Not quite sure that the new iPhone Duo is the right phone for you? I’m also on the fence. Check out CNET’s coverage leading up to the launch of the new foldable and iOS 27, as well as the more conventionally shaped iPhone 18 Pro, so you can make an informed decision.

body: A 39-year-old unvaccinated woman in Franklin County, Pennsylvania, has become the sixth person to die of the highly infectious virus amid a state outbreak that has stricken over a thousand people since it began in April.

The woman died on Saturday, October 10. The advisory noted that the woman's death meets the definition of a measles death set by the state's health department.

articles.headline: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder
keyFacts: Meta released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full on Monday as its first frontier artificial intelligence models.
Meta stated that the new models achieve benchmark scores comparable to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
Meta researchers emphasized the models' active memory feature designed to retain user information over long periods.
body: Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model.

Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.
According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
“Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads.

That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5.
Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent.

In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”

To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark, which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.

“We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch.

The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year. Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.
According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio, which came online earlier this year.
